tracker_name: Global Economic Stress and Resilience Tracker
_schema_note: Append one object to weeks[] per run. Never edit a past week's original scores — add a retrospective_revision instead. See protocol.md Section 17.

indicators.name: Growth momentum
indicators.note: Flash S&P Global Composite PMI rose to an 8-month high (53.6-53.8), consistent with ~2.0% annualized Q3 GDP growth, up from 1.2% in Q2; note the survey window overlaps one-off spending events (FIFA World Cup, USA 250 celebrations) that may be temporarily flattering the reading.

indicators.name: Labor market deterioration
indicators.note: Initial jobless claims fell to 187,000 for the week ending July 18 — the lowest weekly reading of 2026 and lowest since 1969; four-week average also fell, consistent with a still-tight labor market.

indicators.name: Inflation pressure
indicators.note: June CPI (released July 14) cooled to 3.5% y/y headline (core 2.6%), below consensus, driven by falling energy prices. Still well above the 2% target, and the subsequent Iran-conflict oil price surge is a clear upside risk to the next print.

indicators.name: Financial market stress
indicators.note: VIX in the 15-19 range this month (calm-to-mild), 10y-2y Treasury spread modestly positive (+34bps, not inverted). No acute dislocation, but elevated uncertainty ahead of the July 28-29 FOMC meeting and from oil-driven volatility.

indicators.name: Household financial strain
indicators.note: No new NY Fed household debt release this week; most recent data (Q1 2026, reported in May) showed credit card delinquencies at a 16-year high (13.1%) and the highest auto loan delinquency rate on record, even as aggregate household debt ($18.8T) was roughly flat. Distributional stress is building beneath a stable aggregate.

indicators.name: Corporate/banking stress
indicators.note: Major banks (JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, BofA, Wells Fargo, Citigroup) reported Q2 earnings July 14, broadly beating estimates on strong capital-markets activity; no distress signals.

indicators.name: Fiscal stress
indicators.note: FY2026 deficit at $1.4T through nine months, running ahead of FY2025's pace and on track for $2T+ for the year; gross national debt at $39.39T. Average interest rate on marketable debt (3.41%) remains manageable — no auction-demand stress observed — but the trajectory is steadily worsening.

indicators.name: Monetary policy space
indicators.note: Fed funds rate at 3.50-3.75%, giving moderate room to cut if needed, but new Chair Kevin Warsh has taken a more hawkish tone (2026 PCE inflation projection raised to 3.6%) and markets price a 25-30% chance of a hike at the July 28-29 meeting — a credibility transition that adds uncertainty to how much of that space is usable.

indicators.name: Fiscal policy space
indicators.note: Debt service remains manageable at current rates, but the deteriorating deficit trajectory leaves less room for major further countercyclical spending without market pushback.

indicators.name: Banking system soundness
indicators.note: All 32 large banks cleared the Fed's June 2026 stress test, absorbing a hypothetical $708B in losses (10% unemployment, 30% home price decline, 39% CRE decline scenario) with aggregate capital falling only 1.6 points to 11.2%, well above regulatory floors.

indicators.name: Labor market safety net capacity
indicators.note: No new developments this week; standard unemployment-insurance and automatic-stabilizer capacity, unchanged.

indicators.name: External buffers
indicators.note: Dollar strengthened following the Fed's hawkish pivot, reversing a Q2 softening trend; reserve-currency demand for US debt remains intact with no signs of auction stress, though sustained twin deficits are a longer-run pressure on this buffer.

indicators.name: Corporate balance sheet health
indicators.note: Strong Q2 bank and corporate earnings signal healthy balance sheets and no material refinancing-wall stress reported this week.

indicators.name: Household balance sheet health
indicators.note: Aggregate household debt stable and modest, but the same Q1 NY Fed data showing record/multi-year-high delinquencies at the margins means this buffer is bifurcated — comfortable in aggregate, thin for a meaningful subset of households.

weeks.relationship_note: Hard data this week — strong labor market, solid growth, well-capitalized banks — points to a genuinely resilient starting position, but that picture sits above two live risks (an Iran-conflict oil shock threatening the inflation trajectory, and a new, more hawkish Fed chair whose policy credibility is still being tested) that could compress the gap quickly if either worsens.

event_log.description: BLS released June 2026 CPI: headline 3.5% y/y (-0.4% m/m, largest monthly decline since April 2020, driven by falling energy prices), core 2.6% y/y, both below consensus.
event_log.notes: A cooling print, but released before the oil-price surge from the Iran conflict intensified further in the following days — next month's print is a key thing to watch.

event_log.description: JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup reported Q2 2026 earnings, broadly beating estimates on strong capital-markets activity and resilient economic conditions.
event_log.notes: Strong earnings reduce corporate/banking stress (esi_effect: negative) and reinforce banking-system soundness (fri_effect: positive).

event_log.description: China's Q2 2026 GDP growth slowed to 4.3% y/y, the weakest quarterly pace since 2022, below the official 4.5-5% target range, attributed to oil-price effects from the Israel-Iran war and a continued property-sector downturn; exports still surged 27% y/y in June on AI-infrastructure and green-tech demand.
event_log.notes: Global spillover risk: a further Chinese slowdown would weigh on global growth and commodity demand, a factor to track in the 'Growth momentum' indicator going forward even though this tracker is US-anchored.

event_log.description: Initial jobless claims for the week ending July 18 fell to 187,000, the lowest weekly reading of 2026, well under the 212,000 consensus estimate; four-week average fell to 207,500.
event_log.notes: Report date (July 23) falls just after this reporting window, but the reference week (ending July 18) sits within it — included here rather than held for next week since it's the most current labor-market read available.

event_log.description: Brent crude continued to climb toward roughly $86/barrel on renewed Israel-Iran hostilities and Strait of Hormuz shipping attacks, complicating the inflation outlook and Fed policy calculus ahead of the July 28-29 FOMC meeting.
event_log.notes: Forecasts diverge sharply (Goldman sees Brent easing to $80 by Q4; other scenarios range from $40 to $150+ depending on how the conflict resolves) — flagged as the single largest source of uncertainty for next month's inflation and Fed-policy indicators.

weeks.trajectory_note: This is the first tracked week, so there is no prior baseline for week-over-week movement; all changes and arrows are set to zero/steady accordingly. The baseline picture is more favorable than the other two trackers' — a genuinely strong labor market, accelerating growth, well-capitalized banks that just cleared a severe stress test, and cooling (if still above-target) inflation, producing a wide Stress-Resilience Gap of +25. The two things most likely to compress that gap in the coming weeks are external: the Israel-Iran conflict's effect on oil prices, which is a direct threat to the inflation trajectory just as a new, more hawkish Fed chair is establishing credibility ahead of the July 28-29 meeting; and China's slowing growth, a global spillover risk this US-anchored tracker will need to keep watching even though it isn't a primary indicator. A secondary, quieter risk is the bifurcation in household balance sheets — aggregate debt looks calm, but credit card and auto loan delinquencies are at multi-year or record highs for a meaningful subset of borrowers, which a stable aggregate number can mask.

indicators.name: Growth momentum
indicators.note: Q2 GDP advance estimate (BEA, July 30) came in at 1.5% annualized, below the 1.8% consensus and down sharply from Q1's 2.1%; Conference Board consumer confidence (July 28) fell to 90.8, with the present-situation index at its lowest since Feb 2021. Genuine gate crossing (Stable to Warning), reinforced by new blanket tariffs on 60 trading partners adding trade-policy drag risk.

indicators.name: Labor market deterioration
indicators.note: Initial jobless claims ticked up to 197,000 for the week ending July 25 (vs. 188,000 revised prior week) but remain historically low; the four-week average actually fell to 202,750. No payrolls report this week (next release Aug 7) — not a material change, status carried forward.

indicators.name: Inflation pressure
indicators.note: June PCE (BEA, July 30) cooled to 3.7% y/y headline (from 4.1% in May) and 3.3% core — a genuine second straight month of disinflation following June's CPI cooling, though both remain well above the 2% target.

indicators.name: Financial market stress
indicators.note: The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to roughly 4.73-4.75%, its highest since January 2025, and the dollar index rose to 101.64; CCC-rated high-yield credit spreads widened sharply to about 876bps even as investment-grade spreads and the VIX stayed calm (VIX eased from ~20.7 to ~16 intra-week) — a bifurcated but genuine tightening in financial conditions.

indicators.name: Household financial strain
indicators.note: The Q2 Employment Cost Index (BLS, July 31) showed real (inflation-adjusted) wages and salaries fell 0.4% y/y for private-sector workers even as nominal compensation rose 3.3%, reinforcing the strain picture alongside the Conference Board's weakest labor-market differential since February 2021.

indicators.name: Corporate/banking stress
indicators.note: No new bank earnings or supervisory data this week (banks last reported July 14). Corporate bankruptcy filings remain on an elevated multi-year-high trajectory, but that trend was already reflected in prior weeks — status carried forward unchanged.

indicators.name: Fiscal stress
indicators.note: No new deficit, debt-service, or Treasury-auction data released this week; carrying forward last week's reading unchanged. New tariffs on 60 trading partners (10-12.5%, replacing expired duties) and a threatened 35% Canada tariff effective Aug 1 are trade-policy events tracked under Growth momentum rather than this indicator pending any fiscal/revenue data.

indicators.name: Monetary policy space
indicators.note: The Fed held rates at 3.50-3.75% on July 29, but three governors dissented in favor of a hike — the first unified hawkish three-way dissent since September 2016 — signaling reduced internal consensus and testing new Chair Warsh's credibility just as inflation remains above target.

indicators.name: Fiscal policy space
indicators.note: No new deficit or Treasury-auction data this week; carrying forward unchanged.

indicators.name: Banking system soundness
indicators.note: No new bank earnings or supervisory data this week; carrying forward last week's post-stress-test reading unchanged.

indicators.name: Labor market safety net capacity
indicators.note: No new developments this week; unchanged.

indicators.name: External buffers
indicators.note: The dollar index rose to 101.64 (highest since June 25) on the hawkish Fed hold — a continuation of existing reserve-currency demand rather than a new distinct buffer event; no auction-demand stress observed.

indicators.name: Corporate balance sheet health
indicators.note: CCC-rated high-yield credit spreads widened sharply to roughly 876bps this week even as broad investment-grade and BB-tier spreads stayed calm (~281-284bps) — a fresh signal of stress concentrating in the lowest-quality corporate credit tier.

indicators.name: Household balance sheet health
indicators.note: Real wages fell 0.4% y/y per the Q2 Employment Cost Index and Conference Board present-situation confidence hit its lowest level since February 2021, both fresh data points reinforcing the bifurcated household picture.

weeks.relationship_note: A dense month-end data cluster (GDP, PCE, ECI, consumer confidence, FOMC) delivered genuine new evidence this week, and it skewed toward stress: growth decelerated more than expected and financial conditions tightened (higher yields, wider junk-credit spreads, a divided Fed), while resilience buffers softened only modestly — narrowing the Stress-Resilience Gap from +25 to +16 even though the system remains in a favorable-to-resilient position overall.

esi_gates_crossed.why: Q2 GDP advance estimate (1.5%) missed consensus (1.8%) and decelerated sharply from Q1's 2.1%, compounded by consumer confidence falling to a multi-year low in present conditions and new sweeping tariffs on 60 trading partners.

event_log.description: The US imposed new tariffs of 10-12.5% on 60 trading partners (framed as addressing forced-labor violations) as temporary duties expired, and separately threatened a 35% tariff on Canada effective August 1.
event_log.notes: Adds trade-policy uncertainty and cost-push risk to growth and inflation outlooks; no direct fiscal/revenue data yet to score against the Fiscal stress indicator.

event_log.description: Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index fell 1.4 points to 90.8 in July, entirely driven by the Present Situation Index dropping to 114.9 (lowest since Feb 2021); the labor-market differential fell to its weakest since Feb 2021.
event_log.notes: Survey window (July 1-22) overlapped ongoing Middle East conflict; expectations sub-index held flat and stayed below the 80 threshold historically associated with recession risk.

event_log.description: FOMC voted 9-3 to hold the federal funds rate at 3.50-3.75% for a fifth consecutive meeting; three governors dissented in favor of a 25bp hike, the first unified three-way hawkish dissent since September 2016.
event_log.notes: Policy response, not proof of resolved stress; the unusual dissent signals a credibility/consensus test for the newer Fed leadership rather than a direct change in current stress levels.

event_log.description: CCC-rated high-yield credit spreads widened to roughly 876bps while the broader ICE BofA US High Yield Index stayed calm at ~281-284bps and the VIX eased from ~20.7 to ~16 over the week — an unusual divergence between benign broad volatility/credit measures and acute stress in the lowest-quality credit tier.
event_log.notes: Single-segment signal (CCC tier only); also weighs on the Corporate balance sheet health FRI indicator. Worth confirming persistence next week before treating as a trend.

event_log.description: BEA advance estimate: Q2 2026 real GDP grew at a 1.5% annualized rate, below the 1.8% consensus and down from 2.1% in Q1; consumer spending, investment, and exports rose, partly offset by a decline in government spending.
event_log.notes: Advance estimate, subject to revision August 26. Primary driver of the Growth momentum gate crossing from Stable to Warning.

event_log.description: BEA Personal Income and Outlays: June 2026 PCE price index fell 0.1% m/m, with the year-over-year rate cooling to 3.7% from 4.1% in May; core PCE rose 0.1% m/m and was 3.3% higher y/y.
event_log.notes: Cooling partly attributed to a temporary truce-related pullback in energy prices; Fed Chair Warsh said the softer reading did not weigh heavily on the July 29 rate decision. Still well above the 2% target.

event_log.description: Initial jobless claims for the week ending July 25 rose to 197,000, up 9,000 from a revised 188,000 the prior week (below the 201,000 consensus); the four-week moving average fell to 202,750.
event_log.notes: Small week-over-week uptick within a still-historically-low range; not treated as a material change to status.

event_log.description: BLS Q2 2026 Employment Cost Index: compensation costs rose 0.9% q/q (vs. 0.8% expected); private-sector wages and salaries up 3.1% y/y nominally, but real (inflation-adjusted) wages and salaries fell 0.4% y/y.
event_log.notes: Real-wage decline reinforces both the ESI household-strain indicator and depletes the FRI household balance-sheet indicator; labor market described as 'low hiring, low firing.'

weeks.trajectory_note: This week's data was unusually dense — the month-end cluster of GDP, PCE, the Employment Cost Index, consumer confidence, and a live FOMC meeting all landed within a six-day window — and on balance it tilted toward stress. Growth momentum genuinely weakened (a GDP miss plus falling consumer confidence, compounded by a fresh round of tariffs on 60 trading partners), financial conditions tightened at the margin (higher long-end yields, a stronger dollar, and a sharp widening in the lowest-quality credit spreads even as headline volatility measures stayed calm), and household strain deepened with the first real-wage decline reading in some time. Inflation was the one clear bright spot, cooling for a second straight month per the PCE reading, but a divided, more hawkish-leaning Fed complicates how much of that disinflation translates into future rate cuts. Note that data.json's prior entry is Week 29 (July 13-19); no Week 30 entry was produced, so this week's changes and arrows are measured against Week 29 rather than an unbroken prior week, which the confidence rating below reflects. The Stress-Resilience Gap narrowed from +25 to +16 — still a favorable position, but resilience is being tested on more fronts (monetary-policy consensus, junk-credit stress, household real wages) than it was two weeks ago. Key things to watch next: the July jobs report (Aug 7), the next CPI print, and whether the CCC-tier credit spread widening persists or reverses.

indicators.name: Growth momentum
indicators.note: ISM Manufacturing PMI (Aug 3) jumped to 55.6% (from 53.3%, beating the ~54% consensus), the highest since May 2022, with its Employment sub-index back in expansion for the first time in 33 months; ISM Services PMI (Aug 5) held in expansion at 54.1%. Genuinely positive survey data partially offsets last week's GDP miss and tariff overhang, though hard output data hasn't yet confirmed the surveys, so status stays Warning with an improving arrow rather than a full reversal.

indicators.name: Labor market deterioration
indicators.note: Gate crossed (Stable to Warning). July nonfarm payrolls fell 23,000 (BLS, Aug 7) versus +83,000 expected — the first outright monthly decline in some time — with May and June combined revised down 103,000; unemployment ticked down to 4.1% but on shrinking labor-force participation, and average hourly earnings growth slowed to 3.2% y/y, the lowest since May 2021. ADP's July private-payrolls read (Aug 5) rose just 44,000 versus 70,000 expected, reinforcing the same direction; initial claims for the week ending Aug 1 stayed low and below consensus at 199,000, a partial counterpoint.

indicators.name: Inflation pressure
indicators.note: No new CPI print this week (July CPI due Aug 12, outside this window); carrying forward last month's PCE-based reading unchanged.

indicators.name: Financial market stress
indicators.note: Financial conditions eased this week: the VIX fell to roughly 14.9 by Aug 7 (from the 16-20 range last week), the 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.65%, and broad high-yield credit spreads tightened to roughly 271bps, among the tightest levels of the past decade. The move largely reflects markets pricing out a September Fed hike after the weak jobs data rather than a resolved risk backdrop, so it is read as a genuine but policy-linked easing.

indicators.name: Household financial strain
indicators.note: No new NY Fed household-debt data this week (Q2 report due Aug 11); however, the July jobs report's wage figures (average hourly earnings growth slowing to 3.2% y/y, the weakest since May 2021) provide fresh evidence reinforcing the real-wage/purchasing-power strain flagged via last week's Employment Cost Index.

indicators.name: Corporate/banking stress
indicators.note: No new bank earnings, supervisory actions, or bankruptcy data released within this window; carrying forward unchanged.

indicators.name: Fiscal stress

indicators.name: Monetary policy space

Rate-futures markets cut the implied probability of a September hike to roughly 44% from 57% before the jobs report, as the weak labor data reduced the perceived case made by July's three hawkish dissenters — a market-derived shift, not an actual policy action, so status is held at Mixed pending the Fed's next move.

indicators.note: Broad high-yield OAS tightened to roughly 271bps (Aug 6) from about 281-284bps last week, among the tightest (richest) decile of its history. A CCC-tier-specific reading was not confirmed this week, so it's unclear whether last week's sharp CCC-tier widening persisted or reversed — flagged as a data-availability caveat rather than resolved.

weeks.relationship_note: A data-dense week split cleanly between a genuine, multi-source softening in the labor market (BLS payrolls, ADP, wage growth) and a genuine easing in financial conditions and growth surveys (ISM, credit spreads, yields, VIX), leaving the Stress-Resilience Gap only modestly narrower than last week even as markets read the news as clearing the way for the Fed to hold rather than hike in September.

esi_gates_crossed.why: July nonfarm payrolls fell 23,000 versus +83,000 expected, the first outright monthly decline in some time, compounded by a combined 103,000-job downward revision to May and June, wage growth slowing to its lowest pace since May 2021, and a corroborating ADP miss — a genuine, multi-source convergence of new labor-market weakness this week.

event_log.notes: Initial claims remain historically low and below consensus, a partial counterpoint to the weaker payrolls and ADP reads; the rise in continued claims is a milder cautionary signal worth watching.

event_log.description: BLS Employment Situation: July nonfarm payrolls fell 23,000 versus +83,000 expected; May was revised down 66,000 (129,000 to 63,000) and June down 37,000 (57,000 to 20,000), a combined 103,000-job downward revision; unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% on falling labor-force participation; average hourly earnings rose 3.2% y/y, the slowest pace since May 2021; government payrolls fell 53,000.
event_log.notes: Primary driver of the Labor market deterioration gate crossing (Stable to Warning); the scale of the revisions is as significant as the headline miss.

event_log.description: Markets rallied on the soft jobs data: the VIX fell to about 14.9, the 10-year Treasury yield eased to roughly 4.65%, broad high-yield OAS tightened to about 271bps, and the dollar index slipped from about 99.98 to 99.56; the S&P 500 closed at a record high (+0.6%), the Nasdaq rose about 1.3%, and the Dow gained 0.3%, capping a winning week (S&P +3.5%, Nasdaq +5%).
event_log.notes: Easing driven mainly by reduced hawkish-hike odds rather than a resolved risk backdrop; single-week price action, worth confirming persistence next week per protocol's caution on market volatility.

event_log.description: Rate futures markets cut the implied probability of a September Fed hike to roughly 43.9% from 57% before the jobs report, after the weak labor data undercut the case made by July's three hawkish FOMC dissenters.
event_log.notes: Market-implied shift, not an actual Fed decision; status held at Mixed pending the September meeting, consistent with the protocol's rule against treating a policy expectation as a resolved outcome.

event_log.description: The Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee met Aug 4; a Bloomberg report (Aug 7) said Treasury is weighing changes to long-end auction sizes to help temper rising yields amid the growing debt-issuance burden.
event_log.notes: A discussion/process item, not a concrete policy change; flagged for tracking rather than scored as a material move.

weeks.trajectory_note: The week's dominant story was a broad, multi-source softening in the labor market: the July jobs report showed the first outright monthly payroll decline in some time (-23,000 versus +83,000 expected), compounded by a combined 103,000-job downward revision to May and June, wage growth cooling to its slowest pace since May 2021, and the unemployment rate's dip to 4.1% attributable more to shrinking labor-force participation than to hiring strength. ADP's private-payrolls read (44,000 versus 70,000 expected) corroborated the same direction, while initial jobless claims stayed low and below consensus — a partial counterpoint. Together this evidence justified a genuine gate crossing on Labor market deterioration from Stable to Warning. Growth momentum told a more mixed story: both ISM Manufacturing (55.6%, highest since May 2022, with its employment sub-index back in expansion after 33 months) and ISM Services (54.1%) surveys pointed to accelerating activity, a genuine positive counterweight to last week's soft GDP print and tariff overhang, though survey data has not yet been confirmed by hard output figures. Financial markets read the weak labor data as reducing the odds of the hawkish Fed hike three governors pushed for in July — futures-implied September hike odds fell from 57% to roughly 44% — and reacted accordingly: the VIX eased to a calm ~14.9, the 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 4.65%, broad high-yield credit spreads tightened to roughly 271bps, and equities rallied to fresh highs. This is a case of stress and resilience partially offsetting within the same week rather than moving together: the underlying labor-market weakness is not resolved by a more dovish policy path, so the modest narrowing of the Stress-Resilience Gap (16 to 13) reflects real but partial improvement in financial conditions layered on top of genuine new labor-market softening, not a clean turn in either direction. No new inflation, household-debt, bank-supervisory, or deficit data were released this week (July CPI lands Aug 12, the NY Fed's Q2 household debt report Aug 11), so those indicators carry forward unchanged; a separate institutional item — the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee's Aug 4 discussion of possible long-end auction-size changes amid the growing issuance burden — is a fiscal-space item to watch but not yet a policy change. No material new China, Eurozone, or EM-debt spillover data landed within this window. Key things to watch next week: the July CPI print and the NY Fed household debt report, both landing Aug 11-12, plus whether this week's labor-market softening is confirmed or reversed by subsequent data.
